props.title: Snake Island

sections.content: **Snake Island** (2002) falls into the "creature feature" subgenre of horror that saw a resurgence in the late 1990s and early 2000s, following the success of Anaconda (1997). While not reaching the production values of its more famous predecessor, it follows a similar formula of isolated location + deadly serpents + trapped humans. The film belongs to a wave of direct-to-video creature features that included Python (2000) and **Venomous** (2001), capitalizing on audiences' ophidiophobia (fear of snakes).

sections.content: The early 2000s saw a peculiar fascination with snake-themed horror, likely driven by advances in CGI making serpentine movement more believable on screen. **Deep Rising** (1998) and **Lake Placid** (1999) had proven audiences' appetite for aquatic monster movies, while **Komodo** (2000) showed isolated island settings could still deliver effective creature features. **Snake Island** (2002) attempted to combine these elements, though with notably less success than its bigger-budget counterparts. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Snake Horror

Snake horror has a rich history predating modern CGI, with films like **Ssssss** (1973) and **Venom** (1981) relying on practical effects and real snakes. The genre experienced a renaissance with Anaconda (1997), which combined practical effects with early CGI. This led to numerous imitators, including **King Cobra** (1999) and **Boa** (2001), each trying to find new ways to present serpentine threats. **Snake Island** (2002) represents the tail end of this trend, before the genre went completely over-the-top with Snakes on a Plane (2006).
